passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of three different cognitive training protocols on reaction time in adults aged 20–35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, Treatment A that used a visual-spatial memory task, Treatment B that used a verbal working memory task, and a Combined group that received both tasks. Each training session lasted 30 minutes and was conducted twice a week for six weeks. Reaction times were measured using a computerized Stroop task at baseline, mid-intervention, and post-intervention; Table 1 gives the post-intervention means. The data collected showed that the Combined group had the greatest reduction in reaction time, followed by Treatment A, Treatment B, and the Control group. Researchers concluded that multimodal training may produce the most robust improvements in cognitive processing speed.
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time at post-intervention?
explanation: The table shows the Combined group’s mean response time of 460 ms, which is lower than all other groups (Control 520 ms, Treatment A 485 ms, Treatment B 500 ms).
trap: Choosing Treatment A because it is the first active group listed, instead of comparing all four post‑intervention means.

stem: Which experimental design would best isolate the effect of multimodal training on reaction time?

options.A: A within-subject crossover design where each participant receives all treatments in random order
options.B: A between-subjects randomized controlled trial with four parallel groups
options.C: A case-control study comparing participants with and without training
options.D: A longitudinal cohort study following participants over two years without randomization

explanation: Correct: B) Randomly assigning participants to four parallel groups lets the Combined group be compared with each single-task group and with untrained controls, while randomization balances individual differences across groups. Why the others are wrong: A) Training produces lasting learning, so in a crossover the effect of an earlier protocol would carry over into later periods. C) A case-control study is observational and starts from outcomes rather than assigning training. D) Without randomization, groups may differ in confounders such as motivation or baseline speed.
trap: Assuming a crossover design is superior because participants serve as their own controls, ignoring that learned skills carry over between periods.

stem: Calculate the absolute difference in mean reaction time between Treatment A and the Control group.
explanation: Treatment A mean = 485 ms; Control mean = 520 ms. Difference = 520 – 485 = 35 ms.
trap: Confusing a standard deviation with a difference: 45 ms is the Control SD, not the gap between the two means (520 − 485).

stem: If it differed systematically between the four groups, which of the following would be a confounding variable?

options.B: Mean response time on the Stroop task
options.C: Time of day at which each group completed the Stroop task
options.D: The number of groups in the study

explanation: Correct: Time of day affects reaction time and, if it differed by group, would be mixed with the training effect, so it would be a confounder. Why the others are wrong: A) group assignment is the independent variable. B) response time is the dependent variable. D) the number of groups is a feature of the design that cannot differ between groups.
trap: Calling the independent or dependent variable a confounder instead of a third variable linked to both.

stem: Which statement is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The Combined group's mean response time was 60 ms lower than the Control group's.
options.B: Treatment B had a lower mean response time than Treatment A.
options.C: The Control group had the smallest standard deviation.
options.D: The Combined group had the largest standard deviation.

explanation: Correct: 520 − 460 = 60 ms. Why the others are wrong: B) Treatment B (500 ms) was slower than Treatment A (485 ms). C) Control had the largest SD (45 ms). D) Combined had the smallest SD (35 ms).
trap: Assuming the group with the lowest mean must also be the most variable, or confusing the ordering of Treatments A and B.
